verses.translation_literal: A praise, of David. I will exalt you, my God the king, and I will bless your name for ever and ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song of praise — David's. Here is a man who lifts his voice before the throne of heaven: I will raise you high, my God, my King; I will bless your name, and the blessing will not stop, not today, not ever.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Hebrew verse begins with the title, "A praise, of David", which the KJV and its siblings split off as verse 0 and a separate verse 1; the Hebrew counts it as part of the opening line. The word tehillah, "praise", is the Hebrew name for the whole book of Psalms (Tehillim), and this is the only psalm whose heading carries it. Radak notes that the psalm both opens and closes with the word "praise" (verse 21), and that it is the first of the six psalms that end the book.

The actor should hear the royal setting: "exalt" (rum) is what you do to a king, and David, a king himself, calls God "the king" with the article, as the one true king. The KJV "O king" turns the noun into an address; the Hebrew has "my God, the king", a title more than a call. The KJV's "extol" is archaic for what is simply "lift up". Note the pairing: "exalt" (lifting him up) and "bless" (kneeling to him), and the name, not only the person, which in the ancient Near East was the person's reputation made public. "For ever and ever" is le'olam va'ed, "to the age and further", an idiom for the limit of time itself.

philological_notes.note: Polel of rum, 'be high': 'I will make you high', 'raise you up'. The verb belongs to the language of kings and thrones. The KJV 'extol' is the Latin 'lift out'.
'The king', with the article. Ibn Ezra says the mention of the king is the foundation of the whole praise; Radak reads it as 'the king in truth' above all rulers.

verses.translation_literal: In every day I will bless you, and I will praise your name for ever and ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: Every day, every morning that breaks, I will bless you; and when days have run out I will go on praising your name — for ever, and beyond.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is a ladder of two verbs and two times. "Bless" (barakh) is the daily act; "praise" (halal, from which Hallelujah comes) is the one that never ends. Radak assigns the first to this world and the second to the world to come; Ibn Ezra thinks praisers outrank blessers. The reader should hear a daily routine becoming an eternity.

KJV "Every day will I bless thee" is exact; the Hebrew has "in every day", a distributive phrase meaning "each day", with no sense of one big day. The pairing of "bless" with God as object is itself striking: in the ancient world one blesses a superior to receive blessing. Malbim reads it as the blessing flowing down from God and returning, but that is his philosophy, not the plain sense. The repeat of "your name for ever and ever" from verse 1 is deliberate: the psalm circles back to the same words to show that the act has no end.

philological_notes.note: 'And I will praise': halal, to shine, boast, celebrate loudly. The cohortative ending expresses resolve.

verses.translation_literal: Great [is] YHWH and to be praised exceedingly, and to his greatness [there is] no searching.
verses.translation_dramatic: Great is the LORD — great, and worthy of a praise with no ceiling. And his greatness? There is no digging to the bottom of it. No one has ever found the end.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the psalm, the creed in one line: God is great, and therefore praise must be great. The Hebrew rhythm is three beats on the first half, three on the second, with the plain statement of "great" at the front. Note the verb: "to be praised" is a passive participle of halal, from the verse before, so the line answers the vow: I will praise because he is to be praised.

The last words, ein cheker, "there is no search", come from the vocabulary of mining and exploration (as in Job 11:7, "Can you find out the deep things of God?", a parallel the actor can feel without it being cited here). The KJV "unsearchable" captures it well, but the Hebrew is blunter: "his greatness, there is no probing". Ibn Ezra contrasts God with other kings whose greatness has a beginning and an end. The text does not say that God is far from us, only that nothing we do will reach the boundary. Hence praise is the only fitting response.

philological_notes.note: 'Search, investigation', the noun for digging into a thing to find its limit. 'No cheker' means the greatness cannot be traced to its end.

verses.translation_literal: Generation to generation will praise your works, and your mighty deeds they will declare.
verses.translation_dramatic: One generation hands it to the next: your works, passed on in praise; your mighty deeds told over and over, from father to son, from mouth to mouth.
verses.directors_commentary:
From here the psalm widens from one voice to a chain of voices. "Generation to generation" has no verb between the two words; it is the relay itself: dor ledor. Ibn Ezra and Meiri read it as the elder generation telling the next, fathers to sons; Radak adds that the generation that is passing tells the next what it saw in its own days, since the later one did not see it. The verb "praise" is a different one (shabach) from the halal of verses 1–3. Malbim distinguishes it as praising something as an improvement on what went before, which is his own reading.

The KJV "One generation shall praise thy works to another" adds "One" and "to another" to explain the idiom of dor ledor; the Hebrew leaves the relay bare. The KJV keeps the singular verb, as the Hebrew does: "generation ... will praise", the generation as one body. The second half then switches to the plural, "they will declare", so the ear hears a crowd emerge from a single voice. "Mighty deeds" (gevurot) are acts of strength, in the Psalms usually God's saving acts in history, such as the exodus.

philological_notes.note: Piel of shabach, 'commend, laud'. The subject is the singular collective 'generation', so the verb is singular; the Hebrew has no 'one ... another', which English adds to carry dor ledor.
'Your acts of might', from gever, 'strong man'. The plural points to a catalogue of deeds, not to an abstract power. Ibn Ezra links it to the idea that a king is praised for being a warrior.

verses.translation_literal: The splendor of the glory of your majesty, and the words of your wonders, I will meditate.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I — I will turn it over in my mind, I will murmur it aloud: the splendor, the glory, the majesty that clothe you; and the story of your wonders.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker steps back into the first person after the generations of verse 4. The verse is built as a stack of nouns, one on top of another in a construct chain: hadar kevod hodekha, "splendor of glory of your majesty". The three words are close synonyms for royal radiance, and the actor should let each one add weight. The KJV "the glorious honour of thy majesty" turns the noun chain into adjective and noun; the Hebrew has no adjective at all. Notice that Hebrew puts the objects first and the verb last: "splendor... wonders... I will meditate", so that the verb arrives as the settled conclusion.

The verb sicha is not "speak" as in the KJV. It is to muse, to talk to oneself, to ponder aloud, the murmuring of a person lost in thought (Metzudat Zion glosses it as sicha, conversation and speech). ASV "meditate" is closer. Radak links it to what the speaker does with others, as telling; Malbim takes the habitual, half-unconscious character of sicha as the point. "Words of" (divrei) can also mean "matters, things", so the phrase is both the tale of the wonders and the wonders themselves.

philological_notes.note: 'I will muse, meditate, talk over'. It is the language of private reflection spilling into speech, not formal declaration. The KJV 'speak of' loses the inward half.
A chain of three near-synonyms for royal splendor. Malbim distinguishes hod as inner, hadar as outward; that distinction is his own and later than the psalm.

verses.translation_literal: And the might of your awesome [deeds] they will say, and your greatness I will recount it.
verses.translation_dramatic: They will speak of the force of your awesome deeds, the ones that make a man tremble; and your greatness — that I will count out, one by one.
verses.directors_commentary:
The two halves again set "they" against "I": the crowd says, the singer counts. The verb sapar means to count, and the same root gives "scribe" and "book" (sefer): the singer will enumerate, tally the greatness item by item. The KJV "declare" flattens the counting into announcing. The pronoun at the end of the line, "I will recount it" (asapperennah), picks up "your greatness" with a feminine pronoun, a repeated reference the English must carry as "it".

"Awesome deeds" (nora'ot) are literally "fear-inspiring things", from the root yare, to fear. The KJV "terrible acts" has aged badly: today it means "bad", where the Hebrew means "inspiring awe". Ibn Ezra thinks of the signs in Egypt, and Malbim says the crowd fears the punishment while the singer sees only greatness; these are their readings. The written text (Ketiv) of "your greatness" has a plural yod, "greatnesses"; the reading (Qere) is singular. Radak treats the plural as many deeds in human eyes and the singular as unity in God.

philological_notes.note: Niphal participle of yare, 'to fear'; 'the things that are feared, that inspire awe'. The KJV 'terrible' meant this in 1611 but no longer does.
Ketiv gedulotekha (plural), Qere singular. Radak says the plural is how many things look to the human recipient, the singular how they are one in God.
Piel of saphar, 'count, recount, tell in order'. The suffix -ennah is a feminine pronoun with a final nun, 'I will recount it'.

verses.translation_literal: The remembrance of the abundance of your goodness they will pour forth, and your righteousness they will shout for joy.
verses.translation_dramatic: The memory of your great goodness will gush from them like a spring; and your righteousness they will sing out loud, with a shout of joy.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verbs change tone: the first half is a spring, the second a cry. "Pour forth" (yabbi'u) is the word for bubbling, gushing water, and is used in Psalm 19 for "day to day pours out speech", a parallel Metzudat Zion cites. The KJV "abundantly utter" makes the water into a polite speech. The memory here is not recollection of the past only but a public memorial, a remembrance announced aloud.

The second half moves from speech to shouting: yeranenu, "they will give a ringing cry", belongs to public celebration, with the voice raised so that neighbors hear (Radak: aloud, before people). Tsedaqah is "righteousness" and also "generous justice"; in Psalms it often means God acting to put things right for the weak. The KJV "sing of" is decent but loses the loudness. The phrase rav tuvkha, "abundance of your goodness", is a noun plus noun, where English wants an adjective; Radak says rav is a noun here, as if "the size of your goodness".

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of nava', 'to bubble up, gush forth', used of springs. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'speak', citing Psalm 19:3.
Piel of ranan, 'to ring out, shout for joy'. Radak: they will say it in a loud voice before people.

verses.translation_literal: Gracious and compassionate [is] YHWH, long of nostrils and great of covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is gracious, the LORD is tender; he is slow to burn with anger, and wide beyond measure in his faithful love.
verses.directors_commentary:
These are the words God spoke over Moses at Sinai (Exodus 34:6), repeated in the Psalms and the prophets almost like a liturgical formula. The audience would have recognized them instantly, as people recognize a creed. Hanun and rachum, "gracious and compassionate", are the two opening adjectives; rachum is linked to rechem, "womb", so the word carries the mother's tenderness, a link that "full of compassion" (KJV) and "merciful" (ASV) do not show.

"Long of anger" in Hebrew is erekh appayim, literally "long of nostrils". Anger in Hebrew is hot breath through the nose ("his nose burned"); a long nose is slow, patient breathing. The KJV "slow to anger" is right but loses the body. The dual form appayim, "nostrils", is the same word as "anger" (af). Chesed is not "mercy" (KJV "great mercy") but covenant loyalty, the faithfulness that comes from a bond; the whole line therefore says the God who rules is also the God bound to his people. Radak reads "great" as making chesed greater than people deserve.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'long of nostrils', the idiom for patience: anger is hot breath, and a long nose breathes slowly. Radak says it means he extends his anger toward the wicked and does not punish at once.
Covenant loyalty, steadfast love within a bond. 'Mercy' (KJV) suggests only pity; the Hebrew implies obligation freely kept.

verses.translation_literal: Good [is] YHWH to the all, and his compassions [are] over all his works.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is good — to everyone, to everything. His tenderness rests over all that his hands have made.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the widest verse of the psalm, and the scope is the point: "to the all", lakol, with the definite article, is simply everything. The KJV adds "men" nowhere here, but BBE's "to all men" narrows what the Hebrew leaves open. Meiri and Radak both take the verse to include animals and plants; Radak tells how Rabbi Judah the Prince rebuked a servant for sweeping out small creatures from the house, quoting the second half of this verse. Metzudat David reads "all" as good and bad people alike.

The first half is the shortest clause in the psalm: "good is YHWH", with the adjective first. Rachamav, "his compassions", is plural, from rechem, "womb", as in verse 8. The KJV "tender mercies" captures the plural and the warmth. Ancient Near Eastern gods, in contrast, were good to those who fed them; the god of this verse is not tied to a people's offerings. That fits the polemic of the psalm: a king whose kindness covers even those who do not serve him.

philological_notes.note: Plural of 'compassion', from rechem 'womb'; the plural has the sense of repeated, tender acts. Not 'mercies' in the sense of pardon.

verses.translation_literal: They will give thanks to you, YHWH, all your works, and your faithful ones will bless you.
verses.translation_dramatic: All you have made will give thanks to you, LORD; and those who are yours, the faithful, will bless you.
verses.directors_commentary:
Verse 9 spoke of all God's works; verse 10 turns them into singers. The same word, ma'aseikha, "your works", now becomes the subject: creation itself gives thanks. Radak reads it as people seeing the order of living things and thanking God on their behalf; Meiri speaks of those who understand nature. The actor can play it as the world answering.

The verb "give thanks" (hodah) and "bless" (barakh) are distinct, and the KJV renders the first as "praise", flattening the difference. Hodah is public acknowledgment of what someone has done, as in thanksgiving offerings. The second half names a smaller circle: chasidim, "the loyal", people of chesed, which the KJV renders "saints", a word that now suggests canonized holiness; in the Hebrew, the word means those who answer God's covenant loyalty with their own. Radak notes the extra syllable on the verb, yevarakhukhah, with a final ah, "written with the he of rest", an archaic lengthening that gives the line a solemn, drawn-out ending.

philological_notes.note: 'Your loyal ones', those who practice chesed back to God. 'Saints' (KJV) carries later Christian meaning. Radak says the word means those who go beyond, who contemplate God's works constantly.
The pronoun suffix -kha takes an extra he, giving a long, archaic form that Radak says is written with the he for rest.

token_glosses.gloss: they will give thanks to you

verses.translation_literal: The glory of your kingdom they will say, and your might they will speak.
verses.translation_dramatic: They will tell of the glory of your kingdom; they will speak of your strength, and not fall silent.
verses.directors_commentary:
The faithful of verse 10 now do what they came to do: speak. The two verbs, "say" (amar) and "speak" (dibber), are used in parallel to make a rhythm; Malbim, thinking of the piel form of dibber, says it means speaking at length. The two objects are royal: kavod malkhutekha, "the glory of your kingdom", and gevuratekha, "your might". The word malkhut, "kingdom", is the key of the whole psalm and brings back the "king" of verse 1; the psalm now says what the king's rule is. Radak reads the line as saying that God is king over all and creator of all.

The KJV "talk of thy power" is lively, but "power" is a weaker word than gevurah, which is the strength of a warrior. Kingdom here does not mean a territory; it is the act and authority of ruling, "kingship". The KJV ends the verse with a semicolon where the Hebrew sentence runs on into verse 12, because verse 12 states the aim of this telling.

philological_notes.note: 'Your kingship, your reign'. It names the act of ruling more than a territory. The key word of the second half of the psalm, repeated in verses 12 and 13.

verses.translation_literal: To make known to the sons of the human his mighty deeds, and the glory of the majesty of his kingdom.
verses.translation_dramatic: So that every child of Adam may know what he has done in strength, and may see the glory and majesty of his reign.
verses.directors_commentary:
The purpose clause explains the speaking of verse 11: the praise is not for God's benefit, it is to make him known. The verb lehodia is the causative of "know": "to cause to know". The audience is "the sons of the human", benei ha'adam, the whole human race, literally "the sons of the Adam", with the article, an idiom for humankind. Radak says that as the faithful bless in private, so they must announce his power to those who do not know it. Meiri notes that the prophets speak now in the second person and now in the third, which he gives as the reason for the change from "your" to "his".

The KJV "the glorious majesty of his kingdom" turns a chain of nouns into adjective and noun. The Hebrew piles three: kevod hadar malkhuto, "glory of the majesty of his kingdom". The "his mighty deeds" of the first half lines up with "your might" of verse 11, and the "glory of ... kingdom" with the same words there, so verse 12 is a mirror of verse 11 with the audience added. Ibn Ezra explains the "his": the vav of gevurotav, the suffix "his", points back to "your kingdom" in verse 11, which accounts for the switch from "your" to "his".

philological_notes.note: Literally 'sons of the human', the standard idiom for humankind, not only males. The KJV 'sons of men' keeps the form. Ibn Ezra says it stresses that they are small.
Hiphil infinitive, 'to cause to know'. The aim of all the speaking is to inform others, as Radak and Metzudat David say.

verses.translation_literal: Your kingdom [is] a kingdom of all ages, and your dominion [is] in every generation and generation. [Trustworthy [is] YHWH in all his words, and loyal in all his works.]
verses.translation_dramatic: Your kingdom is no kingdom of a season. It is the kingdom of every age, and your rule runs on through every generation, and the next, and the next after that. The LORD is to be trusted in everything he says, and loyal in everything he does.
verses.directors_commentary:
Say this verse as though looking down a long corridor of years. The Hebrew piles up its terms for sovereignty: malkhut, 'kingship', and memshalah, 'dominion', rule that is exercised, not only claimed. Radak and Meiri draw the contrast that carries the verse: the kingship of flesh and blood has a break in it, in the king's life or at his death, and God's has none. Ibn Ezra says the same of every other kingdom. The throne described here is one that nobody inherits and nobody loses. The doubled 'generation and generation' (dor vador) is the Hebrew way of saying 'all of them, one after another', and it picks up the dor ledor of verse 4, so the psalm's relay of generations ends in the king whose rule outlasts them all.

The KJV's 'an everlasting kingdom' flattens a plural: the Hebrew is 'a kingdom of all olamim', all ages or all worlds, which is what Radak and Metzudat David stress. The KJV also turns the noun phrase 'dominion in every generation' into a verb, 'endureth throughout'. The bracketed second sentence is the nun line. The poem is an alphabet acrostic and nun is otherwise absent; most printings of the Hebrew lack the line, while the Dead Sea Psalms scroll and the Greek have it. An actor may choose to speak it or leave a pause where it would stand.

philological_notes.note: 'Kingship, kingdom, reign'. Here the word is repeated in the same clause ('your kingdom is a kingdom of'), which makes the claim sound like a definition. Radak notes that the two halves repeat one idea in different words.
The plural of 'olam, 'a distant time, an age, perpetuity'. 'Kingdom of all ages' is more concrete than 'everlasting'; Metzudat David reads it as 'all worlds'.
'Dominion, rule', exercised authority. Malbim distinguishes it from malkhut: a king rules by the consent of his people, but a mashal rules by strength.

verses.translation_literal: Sustaining [is] YHWH to all the falling, and raising up to all the bent down.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look at who the LORD holds. Not the strong, but the ones who are going down: every one who falls, he steadies. Every back bent double under its load, he lifts straight again.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tone drops here from the throne room to the ground. After a verse about the vast span of kingship, the psalm turns to a king who bends down. Both verbs are participles, so the action is going on now and continues: 'sustaining', 'raising up'. Samakh is to lean on or prop up, as one braces a wall, and zaqaf is to set upright. 'The bent down' (kefufim) are people whose bodies have bowed under debt, hunger, grief or age; the same word recurs in Psalm 146:8. The ancient picture of a good king, in Mesopotamian and Egyptian texts as well, was one who protected the weak, and the psalm gives that role to YHWH alone; Ibn Ezra notes that human kings raise one man by lowering another, and cannot hold everyone.

The KJV's 'upholdeth' is archaic but accurate; 'those that be bowed down' blurs the physical image. Rashi, on this verse, observes that the line beginning with nun is missing from the acrostic because Israel's fall (Amos 5:2, 'fallen, no more to rise') was foreseen, and that David then answered it with 'The LORD sustains all who fall' by the holy spirit. That reading ties the line right to the missing nun.

philological_notes.note: To lean on, support, prop up. It is the verb for leaning a hand on an animal's head in sacrifice. The participle makes it a standing habit of the LORD, not a single rescue.
Those bent down, bowed. Metzudat Zion says it is a word for stooping low, and cites Psalm 146; Metzudat David reads those who have already bent their stature down to the earth.

verses.translation_literal: The eyes of all look expectantly to you, and you, giving to them their food in its time.
verses.translation_dramatic: Every eye is turned toward you, waiting, the way eyes turn toward a door. And you, you give them their food, each in its own time.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a picture of hunger and trust. The 'all' is not only Israel: Radak and Meiri read it as every living creature, which look to the Creator even without knowing it, each by its own nature. The ancient world lived close to the harvest and the rain; a season that came late or not at all meant famine, and the eyes that watch the sky are real. Hebrew has no verb in the second half: 'and you, giving', which makes 'you' emphatic, a turn from the waiting to the one who answers.

The KJV's 'wait upon thee' sounds like serving at table, and 'meat' meant any food in 1611 and now means flesh. The verb yesaberu is from sabar 'to hope, look expectantly', not the familiar shabar 'to break'; the Metzudot read it as hope. 'In its time' (be'ito) is singular: Radak explains that each kind of creature has its own season for its food. The line echoes Psalm 104:27 almost word for word, as Malbim and Metzudat Zion both note.

philological_notes.note: Piel of the verb 'to hope, wait with expectation'. It is not the same word as 'break', though the spelling in an unpointed text is the same. Metzudat Zion links it to Psalm 104:27 ('all of them look to you').
'Their food', whatever each creature eats. Radak lists grass-eaters, seed-eaters and flesh-eaters, so the 'food' is as varied as the creatures.

verses.translation_literal: Opening [obj] your hand, and satisfying to every living [thing] favour/desire.
verses.translation_dramatic: You open your hand. And that is all it takes. The hand opens, and every living thing, the lowing and the winged, the small and the swift, is filled, each with what its own wanting was reaching for.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play the hand, not the speech. The psalmist gives the verse two participles, 'opening' and 'satisfying', with no "Thou" attached; the word 'you' is carried in the ending of the participles and in 'your hand'. The action is continuous: this is not one famous feeding but what God is doing now, every day, as the previous verse's eyes wait for their food. In an economy of rain-fed farming and shepherding, where a failed season meant hunger for people and flocks alike, an open hand is the picture of provision, and a closed hand the picture of famine.

The Hebrew order is: satisfying / to every / living [thing] / ratzon. The KJV, with the ASV and Webster, turns this into 'the desire of every living thing', a genitive that the Hebrew does not write. That is one reading, and the usual one, but the Hebrew puts ratzon as a separate noun after 'every living thing', almost as the thing handed out: God satisfies every living thing with ratzon. Ratzon can mean desire, but also favour, goodwill, acceptance (the same word is used of the 'time of favour'), so the verse can be heard as 'satisfying every living thing with favour'. The traditional commentators lean on 'desire': Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David all take it as each creature getting what it wants according to its own nature, so that the grazer is fed on grass and the predator on flesh. Rashi instead reads 'his goodness, his favour and his blessing', which keeps both senses alive. Malbim takes yet another route, making ratzon the subject that opens God's hand; that is a minority reading, not the plain syntax. The word 'every' is also worth saying out loud: the verse does not say every person or every Israelite, but every living thing, the whole breathing world under the open hand.

philological_notes.note: Noun from ratzah, 'to be pleased, to accept'. It means both what one wants (desire, will) and the goodwill shown toward someone (favour, acceptance). Here it follows 'every living thing' as a separate noun, not as a genitive, so it can be read as what God satisfies with (favour) or what each creature desires (desire). The commentators mostly take 'each creature's desire according to its nature'.

Hiphil participle of sava', 'to be sated': 'causing to be full'. A participle, so the provision is ongoing rather than a single act; the same image of the open hand filling creatures appears in Psalm 104:28.

verses.translation_literal: Righteous [is] YHWH in all his ways, and loyal in all his works.
verses.translation_dramatic: Whatever the LORD does, there is no crooked step in it. He is right in all his ways, and in every work of his hands he is loyal, and faithful to his own.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the feeding of the creatures, the psalm steps back and gives a verdict on God's conduct. 'Ways' (derakhim) are the path of his dealings with the world; 'works' (ma'asim) are what he actually does. Righteous (tzaddiq) is a legal word, in the right before the law, and loyal (hasid) is the word for covenant love, ḥesed, practised. The pair answers a worry the earlier verses raise: why does one creature get wheat and another barley, and why do some live by eating others? Ibn Ezra and Radak both take up that question, and both answer that God's giving is just and also a gift beyond what anyone could claim.

The KJV's 'holy in all his works' misses the sense: the Hebrew is hasid, 'loyal, gracious', not qadosh 'holy'. YLT's 'kind' and the BBE's 'kind' are nearer. Matching the first clause, the nun line in verse 13 carries the same second half, 'loyal in all his works', so the two verses echo each other.

philological_notes.note: From ḥesed, covenant loyalty or steadfast love. Not 'holy' (qadosh). Radak says God supplies what he is not obliged to give; for Meiri it is God's leaning toward mercy.

'Righteous, in the right'. Malbim's reading is that God's governance of the world is just even when the good seem to suffer and the wicked to prosper, because each one's true reward is kept for the world to come.

verses.translation_literal: Near [is] YHWH to all who call him, to all who call him in truth.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is near. Near to everyone who calls his name, to all who call him and mean it.
verses.directors_commentary:
Nearness is the opposite of what a king usually is. A great king in the ancient Near East was reached through layers of officials, gatekeepers and petitioners' fees; Ibn Ezra makes exactly this contrast, saying that a distant king cannot save those who call him. YHWH is near to 'all', the same 'all' that has run through the poem, and the repeated 'to all who call him' says it twice in the style of Hebrew parallelism. 'Call' (qara') is the ordinary verb for shouting for help or invoking a name.

The qualifier 'in truth' (ve'emet) is where the verse hinges. Metzudat David and Radak read it as mouth and heart in agreement, and Ibn Ezra reads it as not calling to test God. The KJV's 'call upon him' is the pious form of 'call him'; the BBE's 'give honour to his name' replaces the plain verb with an interpretation and drops the cry of need.

philological_notes.note: 'In truth, in sincerity', from the root of 'firm, reliable'. For Metzudat David it means 'the heart is the same as the mouth, and does not deny what the mouth says'.
'Those calling him', a participle, the same root as the verb in the next clause. The repetition is deliberate.

verses.translation_literal: The desire of those who fear him he does, and their cry for help he hears, and he saves them.
verses.translation_dramatic: What those who fear him long for, he brings about. Their cry for help reaches his ear, and he hears it, and he saves them.
verses.directors_commentary:
Three verbs in a row, do, hear, save, and the order matters: the desire is met, the cry is heard, the rescue follows. 'Fear' (yire'im) in biblical Hebrew is not terror but reverence, the right posture of a servant before a king. Note the echo of verse 16: there the LORD satisfies the desire (ratzon) of every living creature, and here he does the ratzon of those who fear him, a narrower circle within the wide one. The KJV's 'he will fulfil' and 'will hear' make the verbs future promises; the Hebrew imperfect is the habit, 'he does'.

Shav'ah is not a general 'cry' but a cry for help, the cry of someone in trouble, used for the Israelites in Egypt in Exodus 2:23 (a related noun). The BBE's 'their cry comes to his ears' is near, but it softens the action of hearing, which in Hebrew always leads to acting. Radak adds that 'save' may mean from a trouble that comes on the world or one that comes to atone for guilt.

philological_notes.note: A cry for help, a shout of need. Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as 'their cry' (tza'aqatam).
'Those who fear him', in the sense of reverence. Ibn Ezra contrasts a subject who fears a king, who is content if the king does him no harm, with one who fears God, whose desire God does.

verses.translation_literal: Guarding [is] YHWH [obj] all who love him, and [obj] all the wicked he destroys.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD stands guard over all who love him. And the wicked, every one of them, he brings to an end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm that has been all tenderness ends on a hard edge, and the actor should not soften it. Shomer is a watchman's word: he keeps guard, as a shepherd or a city sentry does. Love (ahavah) joins reverence from verse 19, and Radak and Malbim take 'those who love him' as a higher rung than 'those who fear him', loving without hope of reward or fear of penalty. Over against them 'all the wicked' is stated twice with the same word 'all', matching 'all' for those who love: the verse is symmetrical, the guarded and the destroyed.

The KJV's 'preserveth' and 'destroy' are close. The Hebrew yashmid is the strong verb for annihilation, from the root shamad, as in 'exterminate'. Radak and Meiri read it against Malachi 3:19, the day that burns the arrogant to stubble. Ibn Ezra adds that a human king could not wipe out the wicked in his land, since they might rise against him, but God knows what is hidden. The BBE's 'sinners' for rasha'im loses the legal sense of the guilty, the ones in the wrong.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of shamad, 'to destroy utterly, exterminate'. It is the verb of complete ending, the opposite of 'guard'.
The wicked, those who are guilty in a legal sense: the opposite of tzaddiq 'righteous' in verse 17.

verses.translation_literal: The praise of YHWH my mouth will speak, and let all flesh bless the name of his holiness for ever and ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: The praise of the LORD, my mouth will speak it. And let every living body bless his holy name, now and for ever and ever.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm closes where it opened, with the singer's own voice. It began with 'I will extol you, my God the king' and ends with 'my mouth', then widens to 'all flesh', everyone and everything that has a body. 'Flesh' (basar) is a plain word that includes the creatures fed in verse 15, not only people; Radak limits it to human beings, as the ones who can bless. 'The name of his holiness' is the literal 'holy name', the Hebrew using a noun, 'holiness', where English uses an adjective. The final 'for ever and ever' returns to the opening vow, and to the 'ages' of verse 13, so the poem closes on its own first theme.

The KJV, 'My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord', follows the English order and loses the Hebrew stress: 'the praise of YHWH' comes first, before the verb. The second verb is a jussive, 'let all flesh bless', a call to join, as Metzudat David says: 'all flesh will bless as I do'. The ancient reader would hear the same word ('bless' from the root barakh) that in the opening verses is the singer's own act now asked of the whole world.

philological_notes.note: 'All flesh', every living body. Radak narrows it to human beings; Meiri takes it as the nations in the days of the Messiah, and cites Isaiah 66:23 for 'all flesh shall come'.
A jussive form, 'let it bless', a wish or invitation. It sits between the singer's own vow in the first clause and the call to everyone else.
